Employer liability: vicarious and direct negligence

During an assigned delivery, employee-driver D speeds and injures P. Employer E proves that D was licensed and carefully screened when hired, but E ignored repeated electronic speeding alerts, conducted no follow-up supervision, and had skipped maintenance of brakes whose poor condition also contributed to the collision. E argues that careful selection alone defeats every claim against it. Assess D’s liability, E’s defenses and theories of liability, and E’s possible recourse after payment.

D is liable under Article 2176 if the speeding was negligent and proximately caused P’s injury. Because D was acting within assigned tasks, Article 2180 also makes E primarily answerable unless E proves all the diligence of a good father of a family to prevent the damage. Careful selection alone is insufficient where the facts show deficient supervision. Independently, E’s own causally contributing failure to maintain the brakes may constitute direct negligence under Article 2176, so the Article 2180 defense would not erase that separate basis. To the extent E pays for damage caused by D as its employee, Article 2181 permits recourse against D; it does not automatically shift E’s own direct fault to D.

Eight years after completion, a building collapses and injures a passerby. The collapse was caused jointly by erroneous load calculations in plans drawn by architect A and inferior steel furnished by contractor C; A also supervised construction. There was no lack of necessary repairs or independent fault by proprietor O. The passerby sues O, A, and C two years after the collapse. Under Articles 1723, 2190, and 2192, who is answerable and is the suit timely?

Article 2190 does not make O liable on these facts because it applies when a total or partial collapse is due to the lack of necessary repairs, which the facts exclude. For third-person damage resulting from a construction defect covered by Article 1723, Article 2192 permits suit only against the engineer or architect or contractor in accordance with Article 1723. A is liable for the collapse caused by the defective plans; C is liable for the inferior materials he furnished; and because A supervised construction, A is solidarily liable with C. The collapse occurred within fifteen years after completion and suit was filed within ten years following the collapse, so both periods in Article 1723 are satisfied. Acceptance of the building does not waive these defect-based causes of action.

D’s speeding is the immediate and proximate cause of a collision that fractures P’s leg, although P’s careless street crossing also contributed to the accident. Afterward, competent medical evidence shows that prompt, low-risk treatment would probably prevent permanent disability, but P refuses it without a reasonable explanation and later claims all lost earnings caused by the disability. Does either act by P completely bar recovery, and how should damages be treated?

Not on the stated facts. Because D’s negligence remains the immediate and proximate cause, P’s pre-accident negligence is contributory rather than a complete bar under Article 2179; it reduces recoverable damages under Articles 2179 and 2214. Separately, Articles 2202 and 2203 make D answerable for natural and probable consequences but require P to exercise reasonable diligence to minimize loss. The court may therefore exclude or reduce the portion of later disability and lost earnings shown to have been reasonably avoidable through the refused treatment, while preserving recovery for the original injury and unavoidable consequences. P must explain why reasonable mitigation was not undertaken; the stated absence of a reasonable explanation supports reduction.

Article 32: private actors and judicial exception

A police officer and a private mall security officer jointly carry out an admitted illegal search of P’s locked office and seize papers. A judge had negligently signed the purported authority, but the judge’s act did not violate any penal statute. No criminal case is filed. The private officer argues that Article 32 applies only to government actors, while all three defendants argue that no civil action may proceed without a criminal prosecution. Resolve the Article 32 claims and available relief.

The police officer and private security officer may both be sued. Article 32 expressly covers any public officer or employee or any private individual who directly or indirectly violates or impairs a listed right, including security against unreasonable searches and seizures. The civil action is entirely separate and distinct, may proceed whether or not the conduct is criminal, and is proved by preponderance of evidence; indemnity includes moral damages, and exemplary damages may also be considered. The Article 32 responsibility is not demandable from the judge on the stated facts because the article creates a specific judicial exception unless the judge’s act or omission violates the Penal Code or another penal statute.
Civil Code, Art. 32 and Art. 2219(10); Constitution, Art. III, Sec. 2

Death caused by crime or quasi-delict

A negligently caused death leaves a surviving spouse and children, who prove the decedent’s earning history and seek loss of earning capacity and moral damages. A dependent sibling, whom the decedent was legally obliged to support but who is not an heir, demands eight years of support. How does Article 2206 treat the claims?

Article 2206 permits death indemnity and properly proved loss of earning capacity, and allows the spouse, descendants, and ascendants to recover moral damages for the death. A support recipient who is not an heir may also demand support from the wrongdoer when the statutory conditions exist, but only for a period not exceeding five years as fixed by the court; the sibling cannot obtain eight years under that provision.
